'''''Molinia caerulea''''', known by the common name '''purple moor-grass''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] that is [[native plant|native]] to Europe, west Asia, and north Africa. It grows in locations from the lowlands up to {{convert|2300|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} in the Alps. Like most grasses, it grows best in [[acid soil]]s, ideally [[pH]] values of between 3.5 and 5, however, it can continue to live under more extreme conditions, sometimes to as low as 2. It is common on moist [[heathland]], [[bogs]] and [[moorland]] throughout Great Britain and Ireland. Introduced populations exist in northeastern and northwestern North America.<ref>{{citation|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=MOCA2|title=Molinia caerulea (L.) Moench }}</ref>

The [[Specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''caerulea'' means "deep blue"<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|page=224}}</ref> and refers to the purple spikelets.

==Description==
''Molinia caerulea'' is a perennial [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[bunchgrass]] (tussock-forming), growing up to {{convert|120|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall (taller when sheltered by [[gorse]] and [[Erica (plant)|heather]]), with many closely packed stems. The leaves are coarse, green, taper to a point, long, flat and sometimes slightly hairy on top.<ref>{{cite book |author=C. E. Hubbard |author-link=Charles Edward Hubbard |year=1978 |title=Grasses: a Guide to their Structure, Identification, Uses and Distribution in the British Isles |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |url=https://archive.org/details/grassesguidetoth0000cehu/page/466/mode/2up |page=351}}</ref> Due to the dense [[tussock (grass)|tussock]] it is very resistant to [[heath]] fires. Its [[ligule]] is a ring of hairs, as in heath grass (''[[Danthonia decumbens]]''). The long narrow purple spikelets are a major identification feature – the [[panicle]] is {{convert|15|cm|0|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Cope>{{cite book |last1=Cope |first1=Tom |last2=Gray |first2=Alan |title=Grasses of the British Isles |date=2009 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London}}</ref>

It flowers between July and September, later than any other species.

==Ecology==
The [[caterpillar]]s of some [[Lepidoptera]] use it as a foodplant, e.g., the [[Carterocephalus palaemon|chequered skipper]] (''Carterocephalus palaemon'').

''[[Claviceps purpurea]]'' is an [[Ascomycota|ascomycetous]] fungus which grows on the seeds of purple moor grass.

''[[Purple moor grass and rush pastures]]'' were a United Kingdom [[Biodiversity Action Plan]] habitat, on account of their rarity.<ref>{{cite report|editor=Ant Maddock|title=Purple moor grass and rush pastures|publisher=UK Biodiversity Action Plan - Plan Priority Habitat Descriptions| date=2008| url=https://data.jncc.gov.uk/data/6fe22f18-fff7-4974-b333-03b0ad819b88/UKBAP-BAPHabitats-43-PurpleMoorGrass.pdf}} Originally published in volume=II: Action Plans, Tranche 1, Vol 2, p253, 1995, reviewed in 2007.</ref>

However, in 2025 it was reported that purple moor grass was spreading over Britain and displacing other vegetation in a way characteristic of invasive species, although it is native. Over the previous fifty years it had spread over large upland areas in much of Wales, [[Dartmoor]], [[Exmoor]], the [[Pennines]], the [[Peak District]], [[North York Moors]], [[Yorkshire Dales]] and many parts of Scotland. Areas of moor grass support very little bird or insect life – a characteristic described as a "terrestrial dead zone" or desert – and is difficult for humans to walk through. It is not controlled by herbivores, who will favour other plant species over the grass and will not eat it whatsoever past early summer, when its nutritional value falls heavily. It is also unaffected by disease and the natural successional processes through which grassland typically transitions to other plant communities, such as [[temperate rainforest]].<ref name="molinia guardian">{{cite news| last=Monbiot | first=George | author-link=George Monbiot |work=The Guardian | date=9 June 2025 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2025/jun/09/britain-deserts-dead-zones-purple-moor-grass |title=There's an invader turning huge swathes of Britain into deserts – and these dead zones are spreading}}</ref>

The cause of the spread is largely human activity: incentives to farmers to raise livestock, and the burning of moorland to produce fresh vegetation for animals, have pushed many environments where ''Molinia'' now dominates beyond their capacity to sustain a natural ecological balance. The heavy deposition of nitrogen, which accumulates in rainfall from livestock farming, traffic and industrial sources, and the drainage of naturally-wet peat bogs also contributes. ''Molinia''{{'s}} deep roots protect it from the burning that destroys other, competing, plant species. Most approaches to destroy the invasive ''Molinia''—burning, weedkiller, livestock grazing—only work temporarily, with the moor grass recolonising cleared areas.<ref name="molinia guardian"/> Approaches such as blocking land drainage to restore its moisture levels, planting sphagnum moss to restore peat bogs, planting trees and excluding livestock are being trialled to combat the issue and restore areas overtaken by ''Molinia''.<ref name="molinia guardian"/>

==Cultivation==
''Molinia caerulea'' is cultivated for its [[panicles]] of purple spikelets on yellow stems. In cultivation it grows to {{convert|1.5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|40|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|page=1136}}</ref> Numerous [[cultivars]] have been selected, of which the following have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf|title=AGM Plants - Ornamental|date=July 2017|page=65|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=4 April 2018}}</ref>
